preamble.summary: LXX Zechariah is one of the most frequently cited prophetic books in the New Testament, especially in the Passion narratives. The Triumphal Entry (9:9), the shepherd struck (13:7), the thirty pieces of silver (11:12–13), the one pierced (12:10), and the living waters from Jerusalem (14:8) all feed into Gospel and Revelation theology. Zechariah's Satan at the right hand (3:1) is also a key text for developing NT demonology.
preamble.notable_variants: The 'branch' (anatolē) at 6:12 that shapes Luke's birth-narrative language; the Zion-king-on-a-donkey at 9:9 cited by Matt 21:5 and John 12:15; the thirty pieces of silver at 11:12–13 that Matthew 27:9–10 attributes (strangely) to Jeremiah; the 'one they have pierced' at 12:10 quoted at John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7; the shepherd-struck oracle at 13:7 that Jesus applies to himself at Matt 26:31 / Mark 14:27.
preamble.theological_legacy: Zechariah 9–14 (the 'Deutero-Zechariah' section) supplied the Passion narrative with more of its scriptural framework than any other block of text outside the Psalms and Isaiah 53. Every moment of Holy Week in the Gospels — entry, betrayal-price, striking, piercing, scattering — has a Zechariah text lurking behind it, usually in its LXX form.

renderings.lxx_reading: ὁ διάβολος εἱστήκει ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀντικεῖσθαι αὐτῷ
renderings.mt_rendering: the adversary standing at his right hand to accuse him
renderings.lxx_rendering: the devil stood at his right hand to oppose him
notes: Like 1 Chronicles 21:1, LXX Zechariah 3:1 renders ha-satan as diabolos — consolidating the Greek-Bible identification of 'the satan' with 'the devil.'

The courtroom-accusatory scene of Zechariah 3:1 (Joshua the high priest on trial, diabolos standing to oppose him) is the template for Revelation 12:10's 'accuser of our brothers, who accuses them day and night.' The Greek kategōr ('accuser') in Revelation 12 is a semantic equivalent for the diabolos-function.
Zechariah 3's joshua-accused-then-vindicated narrative is a favorite patristic type for Christ's trial and vindication.

renderings.lxx_reading: ἰδοὺ ἀνήρ Ἀνατολὴ ὄνομα αὐτῷ καὶ ὑποκάτωθεν αὐτοῦ ἀνατελεῖ
renderings.mt_rendering: Here is the man whose name is the Branch. He will branch out from his place
renderings.lxx_rendering: Behold a man whose name is 'Dawn/Rising.' From below him it shall rise
notes: Hebrew tsemach ('branch, sprout, shoot') — the Davidic-Messianic title already familiar from Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15 — is rendered Anatolē (dawn, rising, sunrise, also 'branch/shoot' in botanical usage) in LXX.
Luke 1:78 uses Anatolē as a Messianic title: 'the Anatolē from on high shall visit us.' Zechariah's Benedictus draws on LXX Zechariah 6:12 for the vocabulary.

The double-entendre of Greek anatolē — sunrise and sprout — allowed it to carry simultaneously the Davidic-branch theology of Jeremiah and Zechariah and the light-dawning theology of Isaiah 9 and 60. Luke 1:78's 'dawn from on high' fuses both strands via the LXX word.

renderings.mt_reading: מַלְכֵּךְ יָבוֹא לָךְ צַדִּיק וְנוֹשָׁע הוּא עָנִי וְרֹכֵב עַל־חֲמוֹר
renderings.lxx_reading: ὁ βασιλεύς σου ἔρχεταί σοι δίκαιος καὶ σῴζων αὐτός πραῢς καὶ ἐπιβεβηκὼς ἐπὶ ὑποζύγιον
renderings.mt_rendering: your king comes to you, righteous and delivered, humble, and riding on a donkey
renderings.lxx_rendering: your king comes to you, righteous and saving, gentle and mounted upon a beast of burden
notes: Matthew 21:5 and John 12:15 both cite this verse for the Triumphal Entry. Matthew's version is close to the LXX: 'praus kai epibebēkōs epi onon.' The adjective praus ('gentle, meek') is the same LXX word used of Moses at Numbers 12:3 and in the Beatitude of Matthew 5:5.

The LXX's 'saving' (sōzōn) — active participle — translates the Hebrew nosha, which is a passive niphal ('delivered/saved'). TCR follows the Hebrew passive; the LXX chose active — 'he is saving.' The shift from passive to active Messianic savior is theologically consequential: the king comes not as one delivered by God but as one delivering others.

John 12:15 shortens the citation dramatically and adds a first-line ('Fear not, daughter of Zion') that matches neither MT nor Rahlfs LXX exactly. Both Matthean and Johannine versions depend on the LXX's base vocabulary.

renderings.lxx_reading: τριάκοντα ἀργυροῦς … κάθες αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸ χωνευτήριον
renderings.mt_rendering: thirty pieces of silver … Throw it to the potter
renderings.lxx_rendering: thirty silver pieces … cast them into the smelter
notes: The LXX reads 'smelter / foundry' (chōneutērion) rather than 'potter' (yotser). The Hebrew consonants y-ts-r can be vocalized either way — yotser is 'potter,' otsar is 'treasury.' The LXX reads a third possibility, perhaps reflecting a variant Hebrew text.

Matthew 27:9–10 famously cites the thirty-pieces-of-silver-and-the-potter passage but attributes it to Jeremiah, not Zechariah: 'then what was said through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled.' The Matthean citation appears to be a composite of Zechariah 11:12–13 (the silver and the potter) with Jeremiah 19 or 32 (the potter and the field-purchase).

The attribution to Jeremiah rather than Zechariah is a puzzle that has exercised commentators since Origen. The most plausible explanation is anthological citation — Matthew names the more prominent prophet whose Scroll contained related material on potters and purchases.

renderings.lxx_reading: καὶ ἐπιβλέψονται πρός με ἀνθ᾽ ὧν κατωρχήσαντο
renderings.mt_rendering: They will look on me — the one they have pierced
renderings.lxx_rendering: They will look at me because they have danced in triumph (mocked)
notes: The LXX misreads Hebrew dqaru ('they pierced') as rqadu ('they danced'). The verb roots d-q-r and r-q-d differ only in the order of two consonants, and the LXX translator saw 'danced' rather than 'pierced.'

This is the clearest case in the Minor Prophets of the LXX differing materially from a Hebrew reading that the NT independently preserves. John 19:37 ('they will look on the one whom they have pierced') and Revelation 1:7 ('every eye will see him, even those who pierced him') both cite the verse in its Hebrew sense (pierced) — against the standard LXX.

This confirms that the NT authors knew the Hebrew, or knew a Greek revision (Theodotion, Aquila) that corrected the LXX back toward the Hebrew. Theodotion Zechariah 12:10 reads exekentēsan ('they pierced'), which is exactly what John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 use.
This verse is one of the signal pieces of evidence that NT writers did not simply use standard LXX — they had access to Greek revisions that brought the Greek closer to the Hebrew.

renderings.lxx_reading: πατάξατε τοὺς ποιμένας καὶ ἐκσπάσατε τὰ πρόβατα
renderings.mt_rendering: Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
renderings.lxx_rendering: Strike the shepherds, and draw out the sheep
notes: Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27 both cite this verse when Jesus predicts his disciples' flight at Gethsemane: 'Strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.' The citation uses the singular 'shepherd' (against the LXX plural 'shepherds') and 'scattered' (diaskorpisthēsontai) where the LXX has 'draw out.'

The Gospels' form agrees with MT (singular shepherd, scattered sheep) rather than the LXX. This is another case where the NT quotation preserves the Hebrew reading against the standard LXX, suggesting a pre-NT Greek revision (Theodotion has similar wording) or direct knowledge of the Hebrew.

The Messianic reading of Zechariah 13:7 — God himself strikes his own shepherd — is theologically daring and became central to Christian Passion theology. Jesus' self-application of the text at the Last Supper makes the verse the key hermeneutical link between the prophet and the Passion.
